title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: The last of the infantry hurried across the bridge, bunching tighter as they neared it, as if squeezing through a funnel. Finally all the baggage wagons had crossed, the crowding eased, and the last battalion reached the bridge. Now only Denisov's squadron of hussars remained on the far side, facing the enemy. The French could be seen from the hill on the opposite bank but were not yet visible from the bridge itself, because the horizon as viewed from the river valley was formed by rising ground barely half a mile away. At the foot of the hill stretched wasteland where a few groups of Cossack scouts were moving about. Then suddenly, on the road at the top of the high ground, artillery and troops in blue uniforms appeared. These were the French. A group of Cossack scouts trotted back down the hill. All the officers and men of Denisov's squadron tried to talk about other things and look elsewhere, but every one of them was thinking only about what was up on that hilltop, and they kept glancing at the shapes appearing on the skyline—shapes they knew to be enemy troops. The weather had cleared again since midday, and the sun was sinking brightly over the Danube and the dark hills surrounding it. It was quiet, and at intervals the sound of bugle calls and shouting from the enemy drifted down from the hill. Between the squadron and the enemy there was now nothing but a handful of scattered skirmishers. An empty stretch of about seven hundred yards was all that separated them. The enemy had stopped firing, and that stern, menacing, untouchable line dividing two hostile armies could be felt more sharply than ever.

One step beyond that invisible boundary—which feels like the line between the living and the dead—lies uncertainty, suffering, and death. And what is over there? Who is over there? Beyond that field, that tree, that sunlit rooftop? No one knows, but you want to know. You are afraid to cross that line, and yet you long to cross it, knowing that sooner or later you must, and that you will have to discover what lies on the other side—just as you will inevitably have to learn what lies beyond death. But you are strong, healthy, cheerful, and keyed up, surrounded by others who are just as excited and alive. That is what anyone thinks, or at least feels, when they come within sight of the enemy, and that feeling lends a special intensity and joyful sharpness to everything that happens in such moments.

On the high ground where the enemy stood, a puff of cannon smoke rose and a ball came whistling over the heads of the hussar squadron. The officers who had been clustered together rode off to their positions. The hussars carefully straightened their formation. Silence fell over the entire squadron. Every man watched the enemy ahead and the squadron commander, waiting for the order. A second cannonball flew past, then a third. They were clearly aiming at the hussars, but each ball whistled rapidly overhead and landed somewhere beyond. The hussars didn't turn around, but at the sound of each shot—as if on command—the whole squadron, with its rows of faces so alike and yet so different, rose slightly in the stirrups, held its breath while the ball passed, and then settled back. Without turning their heads, the soldiers stole glances at each other, curious to read their comrades' reactions. On every face, from Denisov's down to the bugler's, the same expression showed around the chin and mouth: a mixture of tension, irritation, and excitement. The quartermaster glared at his men as though threatening punishment. Cadet Mironov flinched every time a ball flew past. Rostov, on the left flank astride his horse Rook—a handsome animal despite its lame leg—wore the happy look of a schoolboy called up for an exam before a large audience, confident he's going to shine. He kept glancing around with a bright, clear expression, as if inviting everyone to notice how calm he was under fire. But despite himself, that same hint of something new and serious showed around his mouth too.
"Who's ducking over there? Cadet Miwonov! That's not wight! Look at me!" Denisov called out. Unable to stay still, he kept wheeling his horse back and forth in front of the squadron.

The black, hairy, snub-nosed face of Vaska Denisov, and his whole short, sturdy frame with its sinewy hand and stubby fingers gripping the hilt of his bared saber, looked just as it always did—especially toward evening when he'd emptied his second bottle. He was only redder than usual. With his shaggy head thrown back the way birds do when they drink, pressing his spurs ruthlessly into the flanks of his good horse Bedouin, sitting as if he were falling backward in the saddle, he galloped to the other end of the squadron and shouted in a hoarse voice for the men to check their pistols. Then he rode up to Kirsten. The staff captain, on his broad-backed, steady mare, came toward him at a walk. His face with its long mustache was as serious as ever; only his eyes were brighter than usual.
"Well, what do you think?" Kirsten said to Denisov. "It won't come to a fight. Watch—we'll pull back."
"The devil only knows what they're up to!" Denisov muttered. "Ah, Wostov!" he cried, catching sight of the cadet's bright face. "You've finally got your chance!"
He smiled approvingly, clearly pleased with the young man. Rostov felt completely happy. Just then the commander appeared on the bridge. Denisov galloped up to him.
"Your excellency! Let us attack them! I'll dwive them off!"

"Attack, indeed!" the colonel said in a bored voice, scrunching his face as though swatting away a fly. "And why are you standing here? Can't you see the skirmishers are pulling back? Lead the squadron out."

The squadron crossed the bridge and moved out of range without losing a single man. The second squadron, which had been in the front line, followed them across, and the last Cossacks withdrew from the far bank.

The two Pavlograd squadrons, having crossed the bridge, retired up the hill one after the other. Their colonel, Karl Bogdanich Schubert, rode up to Denisov's squadron and proceeded at a walking pace near Rostov, without taking any notice of him—even though this was their first encounter since the incident with Telyanin. Rostov, feeling that he was at the front and in the power of a man toward whom he now admitted he'd been in the wrong, kept his eyes fixed on the colonel's athletic back, his light-haired nape, and his red neck. It struck Rostov that Bogdanich was only pretending not to notice him, and that his real purpose was to test the cadet's courage. So he straightened up and looked around cheerfully. Then it seemed to him that Bogdanich was riding so close on purpose, to show off his own bravery. Next he imagined that the colonel would send the squadron on some desperate charge just to punish him—Rostov. And then he pictured how, after the charge, Bogdanich would approach him as he lay wounded and magnanimously extend the hand of reconciliation.

The high-shouldered figure of Zherkov, familiar to the Pavlograds since he'd only recently left their regiment, rode up to the colonel. After being removed from headquarters, Zherkov hadn't stayed with the regiment, claiming he wasn't fool enough to toil at the front when he could earn more rewards by doing nothing on the staff. He had managed to attach himself as an orderly officer to Prince Bagration. Now he came to his former commander with an order from the rear guard.
"Colonel," he said, addressing Rostov's enemy with an air of solemn gravity, glancing around at his former comrades, "there's an order to halt and set fire to the bridge."
"An order from whom?" the colonel asked sourly.
"I don't exactly know 'from whom,'" the cornet replied in a serious tone, "but the prince told me: 'Go and tell the colonel that the hussars must return at once and burn the bridge.'"

Behind Zherkov came another officer from the suite, riding up to the hussar colonel with the same order. After him, the stout Nesvitski came galloping up on a Cossack horse that could barely carry his weight.

"Colonel, what's going on?" he shouted as he approached. "I told you to set fire to the bridge, and now someone's gone and botched it. Everyone over there is in a panic and nobody can figure out what's happening."
The colonel deliberately halted the regiment and turned to Nesvitski.
"You spoke to me about inflammable material," he said, "but you said nothing about setting fire to it."

"But my dear sir," said Nesvitski, reining in and taking off his cap to smooth his sweat-dampened hair with his plump hand, "wasn't I telling you to burn the bridge after the inflammable material had been placed?"

"I am not your 'dear sir,' Mister Staff Officer, and you did not tell me to burn the bridge! I know my duty, and I make it my habit to follow orders strictly. You said the bridge would be burned—but who was supposed to burn it? I couldn't know that by divine inspiration!"
"It's always the same!" Nesvitski said with a wave of his hand. "How did you end up here?" he asked, turning to Zherkov.
"Same errand. But you're soaking wet! Let me wring you out!"
"You were saying, Mister Staff Officer..." the colonel continued in an offended tone.
"Colonel," the officer from the suite cut in, "you need to move quickly, or the enemy will bring up their guns for grapeshot."
The colonel looked silently at the suite officer, then at the stout staff officer, then at Zherkov, and he frowned.
"I vill ze bridge fire," he announced in a solemn tone, as if to declare that despite all the aggravation he was enduring, he would still do the right thing.

Striking his horse with his long, muscular legs as though the animal were to blame for everything, the colonel rode forward and ordered Denisov's squadron—the second, in which Rostov was serving—to return to the bridge.
"There it is—just as I thought," Rostov said to himself. "He wants to test me!" His heart clenched and the blood rushed to his face. "Let him see whether I'm a coward!" he thought.

Once again, the grave expression the men had worn under fire settled over every bright face in the squadron. Rostov kept watching his enemy, the colonel, closely, searching his face for confirmation of his suspicions. But the colonel never once glanced at Rostov and looked just as he always did at the front—solemn and stern. Then came the word of command.
"Quick! Quick!" several voices repeated around him.

Sabers catching on bridles and spurs jingling, the hussars hastily dismounted, none of them quite sure what they were supposed to do. The men were crossing themselves. Rostov no longer looked at the colonel—there was no time. He was terrified of falling behind the others, so terrified that his heart seemed to stop. His hand shook as he handed his horse off to an orderly, and he felt the blood pound against his chest. Denisov rode past him, leaning back and shouting something. Rostov saw nothing but hussars running all around him, their spurs catching and sabers clanking.
"Stretchers!" someone shouted behind him.

Rostov didn't stop to think about what that call meant. He just ran, trying to stay ahead of everyone. But right at the bridge, not watching his feet, he stepped into some sticky, trampled mud, stumbled, and fell on his hands. The others rushed past him.
"At both sides, Captain," he heard the colonel's voice. Bogdanich had ridden ahead and pulled up his horse near the bridge, his face triumphant and cheerful.

Rostov wiped his muddy hands on his trousers, looked at his enemy, and was about to run forward again, thinking the further ahead he got, the better. But Bogdanich, without looking at him or showing any sign of recognition, shouted:
"Who's running down the middle of the bridge? To the right! Come back, Cadet!" he shouted angrily. Then, turning to Denisov, who had ridden out onto the bridge planks to show off his courage:
"Why take unnecessary risks, Captain? You should dismount," he said.
"Every bullet has its target," Vaska Denisov replied, turning in his saddle.

Meanwhile, Nesvitski, Zherkov, and the officer from the suite stood together out of range, watching—now the small cluster of men in yellow shakos, dark-green braided jackets, and blue riding trousers swarming around the bridge, and now what was approaching from the far side: blue uniforms and groups of men with horses, clearly recognizable as artillery.

"Will they manage to burn the bridge or not? Who'll get there first? Will they set it ablaze, or will the French get close enough for grapeshot and wipe them out?" Every man watching from the high ground above the bridge was asking himself these questions with a sinking heart, gazing at the bridge and the hussars in the bright evening light and the blue-coated troops advancing from the other side with bayonets and guns.
"The hussars are going to catch it!" Nesvitski said. "They're within grapeshot range now."
"He shouldn't have taken so many men," the officer from the suite remarked.
"That's true enough," Nesvitski agreed. "Two quick fellows could have done the job just as well."

"Ah, your excellency," Zherkov put in, his eyes fixed on the hussars but still wearing that guileless look that made it impossible to tell whether he was joking or serious. "How you look at things! Send two men? But then who would earn the Vladimir medal and ribbon? As it is, even if they do get peppered, the squadron can be put up for honors and he can win a ribbon. Our Bogdanich knows how things are done."
"There!" said the officer from the suite. "That's grapeshot."
He pointed to the French guns, whose limbers were being hurriedly detached and pulled away.

On the French side, a cloud of smoke rose from one of the gun positions, then a second and a third almost simultaneously. At the moment the first report reached them, a fourth flash was visible. Then two booms in quick succession, and a third.
"Oh! Oh!" Nesvitski groaned as if in sharp pain, grabbing the officer from the suite by the arm. "Look! A man's gone down! Down, down!"
"Two, I think."
"If I were Tsar, I would never go to war," Nesvitski said, turning away.

The French guns were hastily reloaded. The infantry in blue advanced toward the bridge at a run. Smoke appeared again in irregular bursts, and grapeshot crackled and rattled against the bridge. But this time Nesvitski couldn't see what was happening there—a dense cloud of smoke had risen from the bridge. The hussars had managed to set it on fire, and the French batteries were now shooting at them not to stop them, but simply because the guns were aimed and there were targets to hit.

The French managed to fire three rounds of grapeshot before the hussars made it back to their horses. Two of the rounds went wide, the shot sailing too high, but the last one landed in the middle of a cluster of hussars and knocked three of them down.

Rostov, preoccupied with his feelings about Bogdanich, had stopped on the bridge with no idea what to do. There was no one to cut down—he had always imagined battles with saber in hand—and he couldn't help burn the bridge since he hadn't brought any burning straw like the other soldiers. He just stood there looking around, when suddenly he heard a rattling sound on the bridge, like nuts being spilled, and the hussar nearest to him fell against the railing with a groan. Rostov rushed over with the others. Again someone shouted, "Stretchers!" Four men grabbed the hussar and began lifting him.
"Oh God! For Christ's sake, leave me alone!" the wounded man cried, but they lifted him anyway and placed him on the stretcher.

Nikolai Rostov turned away and gazed into the distance, as if searching for something—at the waters of the Danube, at the sky, at the sun. How beautiful the sky was: how blue, how calm, how deep! How bright and glorious the setting sun! How softly the distant waters of the Danube glittered! And more beautiful still were the far-off blue mountains beyond the river, the convent, the mysterious gorges, the pine forests veiled in mist at their summits... There was peace there, and happiness... "I would want nothing else, nothing at all, if only I were there," Rostov thought. "In me alone and in that sunshine there is so much happiness. But here... groans, suffering, fear, and this chaos and rush... Over there—they're shouting again, and again everyone is running somewhere, and I'll run with them, and it—death—is here, above me and all around me... One more instant, and I will never again see this sun, this water, that gorge!..."

At that moment the sun began to slip behind the clouds, and more stretchers came into view before Rostov. And the fear of death and of the stretchers, and the love of the sun and of life, all merged into a single feeling of nauseating dread.
"Oh Lord God! You who are in that heaven—save me, forgive me, and protect me!" Rostov whispered.
The hussars ran back to the men holding their horses. Their voices grew louder and calmer. The stretchers disappeared from sight.
"Well, fwiend? So you've had a taste of gunpowder!" Vaska Denisov shouted right above his ear.
"It's all over—but I'm a coward. Yes, a coward!" Rostov thought, and with a deep sigh he took Rook from the orderly—the horse was standing with one hoof resting—and began to mount.
"Was that grapeshot?" he asked Denisov.

"You bet it was!" Denisov cried. "You all worked like real heroes, and it's nasty business! A charge is good work—hacking away at the enemy! But this kind of thing is pure hell, with them shooting at you like you're a target."
Denisov rode up to a group that had gathered near Rostov, made up of the colonel, Nesvitski, Zherkov, and the officer from the suite.
"Well, it seems no one noticed," Rostov thought. And it was true. No one had paid any attention, because everyone understood the sensation that a cadet experiences under fire for the first time.
"Here's something for you to report," said Zherkov. "Watch—I'll get promoted to sub-lieutenant for this."
"Inform ze prince zat I ze bridge fired!" the colonel declared, triumphant and beaming.
"And if he asks about the losses?"

"A trifle," the colonel said in his deep bass voice. "Two hussars wounded, and one knocked out." He couldn't hold back a satisfied smile, and he pronounced the words "knocked out" with ringing clarity.
